Issued at 451 AM CDT Fri Jul 31 2026

A shortwave trough is located over the eastern 
Dakotas/Minnesota early this morning. The associated surface low
is analyzed near Sioux Falls, with a broad high pressure ridge 
from northern Saskatchewan through western North Dakota. Shower 
and thunderstorm activity has shifted well off to the southeast.
Patchy fog remains possible along the surface ridge axis in 
western North Dakota early this morning, but little to none has 
been observed as of this writing. The surface ridge is forecast 
to slide into central North Dakota this afternoon as the 
downstream shortwave digs southeastward along the lower Missouri
River Valley. There is a low-amplitude shortwave traveling 
along the top of the upper level ridge over central Montana 
early this morning that is responsible for showers and isolated 
thunderstorms. Models tend to dissolve and slow the progression 
of this shortwave as it approaches western North Dakota, but it 
appears to be more potent and progressive on water vapor 
imagery. There is a low chance that this wave could bring a few 
showers or thunderstorms to western parts of the state today, 
but the forcing will be running into rising mid level height 
tendencies, as well as the surface ridge. Only a narrow ribbon 
of no greater than 1000 J/kg CAPE is forecast across far western
North Dakota through this evening, and model soundings would 
indicate mid level capping should prevent convection from 
becoming surface or mixed-layer based. If an updraft were to 
become rooted in the boundary layer, it would experience 
effective bulk shear around 35-40 kts. The 00Z HREF does still 
have a contour of 10 percent in its neighborhood probability of 
updraft helicity exceeding 75 m^2/s^2, but almost the entire 
contribution to that appears to be from 12Z initialized members.
It is therefore highly unlikely that there will be any stronger
storms today, although inverted-v thermodynamic profiles could 
support gusty winds with even just showers. But the probability 
of any showers or storms in western North Dakota today remains 
under 20 percent. Those chances do increase slightly and shift 
into north central North Dakota tonight as the low level jet 
increases and turns to point northeastward, inducing warm air 
advection. But any overnight activity would likely be limited to
just showers as forecast CAPE over north central North Dakota 
tonight remains very low.

With North Dakota sitting between a downstream trough and 
upstream ridge today, high temperatures are forecast to be 
limited to the lower and mid 80s east but reach the lower 90s 
west. Over the course of the weekend, the upper ridge will once 
again become highly amplified and pivot into a positive tilt as 
a potent upper low digs into British Columbia. The thermal ridge
expands into western North Dakota on Saturday where highs could
approach 100, then gets shoved over central North Dakota on 
Sunday as the British Columbia low ejects into the Canadian 
prairie and drives a cold front into western North Dakota. 
Recent NBM guidance has trended slightly cooler with 
temperatures both days this weekend, with daily maxima 
projections now closer to 100 rather than 105. But still think 
compressional heating ahead of the cold front could produce a 
corridor of ~105 degree Fahrenheit temperatures over south 
central North Dakota Sunday afternoon. We will continue to 
message heat concerns this weekend, but the latest trends 
paired with it being a drier air mass may preclude the need for
any headlines. The other concern for Sunday is that windy 
conditions both ahead of the front (south winds around 25 mph 
gusting to 40 mph) and behind the front (northwest around 20 mph
gusting to 30 mph) will combine with the hot and dry air to 
produce at least near-critical fire weather conditions across 
much of the western half of the state. The current forecast 
calls for only around 1 to 3 hours of meeting Red Flag criteria,
and only on a limited basis spatially. But the wind shift with 
the frontal passage and very hot temperatures are factors that 
will need to be considered. As it stands now, there is still 
enough uncertainty in the magnitude of winds and the timing of 
the cold front to preclude the issuance of a Fire Weather Watch,
but this could easily change with future forecast updates.

The cold front is forecast to temporarily stall from northeast 
to south central North Dakota Sunday night into Monday as the 
Canadian low occludes and a separate shortwave lands on the 
American side of the Pacific Northwest. The cold front itself 
is unlikely to be able to initiate convection during the day 
Sunday as it moves through a high CIN and low RH environment, 
but some sets of model guidance introduce QPF late Monday night 
as stronger mid level height falls commence over the region and 
flow aloft turns southwesterly with embedded shortwave energy. 
Effective bulk shear can be tricky to forecast for elevate
